### V-238334 · UBTU-20-010413 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must disable kernel core dumps so that it can fail to a secure state if system initialization fails, shutdown fails or aborts fail.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-238334r958550_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000184-GPOS-00078 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations, Boot Process & Console Security |
| CCI | CCI-001190 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-24 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-24 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-24 |
| Implemented via | Service (systemd) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable kernel core dumps so that it can fail to a secure state if system initialization fails, shutdown fails or aborts fail.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Service | systemd | kdump.service | disable |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
systemctl is-active kdump.service
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
systemctl is-enabled kdump.service; systemctl is-active kdump.service
```

Expected: Expect disabled / inactive.

**How it works:** Set kernel tunables in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf and apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Boot parameters are added to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub, followed by 'update-grub' and a reboot. Disable core dumps through /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard core 0') and /etc/systemd/coredump.conf.

**Also related (Boot Process & Console Security):** Create a GRUB superuser password hash with 'grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2' and add 'set superusers="<name>"' and 'password_pbkdf2 <name> <hash>' to /etc/grub.d/40_custom (or 00_header), then run 'update-grub'. Kernel parameters go in GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub, followed by 'update-grub'. Disable Ctrl-Alt-Delete with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'systemctl daemon-reload'.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that kernel core dumps are disabled unless needed.

Check if "kdump" service is active with the following command:

$ systemctl is-active kdump.service
inactive

If the "kdump" service is active, ask the SA if the use of the service is required and documented with the ISSO.

If the service is active and is not documented, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
If kernel core dumps are not required, disable the "kdump" service with the following command:

$ sudo systemctl disable kdump.service

If kernel core dumps are required, document the need with the ISSO.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Kernel core dumps may contain the full contents of system memory at the time of the crash. Kernel core dumps may consume a considerable amount of disk space and may result in denial of service by exhausting the available space on the target file system partition.

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution; T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001190**: Fail to an organization-defined known-system state for the list of organization-defined types of system failures on organization-defined system components on the indicated components while preserving organization-defined system state information in failure.  
  Rev 5: SC-24 · Rev 4: SC-24 · Rev 3: SC-24

### V-238335 · UBTU-20-010414 · CAT II: Ubuntu operating systems handling data requiring "data at rest" protections must employ cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure and modification of the information at rest.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-238335r958552_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000185-GPOS-00079 |
| Topic | Data-at-Rest Encryption |
| CCI | CCI-001199, CCI-002475, CCI-002476 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-28, SC-28 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-28, SC-28 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-28 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer handling data requiring "data at rest" protections must employ cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure and modification of the information at rest.

**Why it matters:** This scrambles everything stored on the computer's drive so it can only be read after the right key or PIN is entered at startup. If someone steals the laptop or pulls out the hard drive, all they get is gibberish. It's like keeping your documents in a locked safe instead of a cardboard box.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
more /etc/crypttab
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Ubuntu uses LUKS (dm-crypt) for block-device encryption, normally chosen at install time ('Encrypt the new Ubuntu installation'). Retrofitting encryption to an existing root volume generally requires a rebuild. Verify with 'lsblk -f' or 'cryptsetup status <mapping>'.

**Operational impact:** Requiring a pre-boot PIN means unattended reboots (patch windows, remote power-cycles) stop at the PIN prompt unless Network Unlock is deployed. Plan key escrow and helpdesk recovery procedures before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If there is a documented and approved reason for not having data-at-rest encryption, this requirement is Not Applicable.

Verify the Ubuntu operating system prevents unauthorized disclosure or modification of all information requiring at-rest protection by using disk encryption.

Determine the partition layout for the system with the following command:

#sudo fdisk -l
(..)
Disk /dev/vda: 15 GiB, 16106127360 bytes, 31457280 sectors
Units: sectors of 1 * 512 = 512 bytes
Sector size (logical/physical): 512 bytes / 512 bytes
I/O size (minimum/optimal): 512 bytes / 512 bytes
Disklabel type: gpt
Disk identifier: 83298450-B4E3-4B19-A9E4-7DF147A5FEFB

Device       Start      End  Sectors Size Type
/dev/vda1     2048     4095     2048   1M BIOS boot
/dev/vda2     4096  2101247  2097152   1G Linux filesystem
/dev/vda3  2101248 31455231 29353984  14G Linux filesystem
(...)

Verify the system partitions are all encrypted with the following command:

# more /etc/crypttab

Every persistent disk partition present must have an entry in the file.

If any partitions other than the boot partition or pseudo file systems (such as /proc or /sys) are not listed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
To encrypt an entire partition, dedicate a partition for encryption in the partition layout.

Note: Encrypting a partition in an already-installed system is more difficult because it will need to be resized and existing partitions changed.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Information at rest refers to the state of information when it is located on a secondary storage device (e.g., disk drive and tape drive, when used for backups) within an operating system.

This requirement addresses protection of user-generated data, as well as operating system-specific configuration data. Organizations may choose to employ different mechanisms to achieve confidentiality and integrity protections, as appropriate, in accordance with the security category and/or classification of the information.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000404-GPOS-00183, SRG-OS-000405-GPOS-00184

**Threat & control context:** Full-volume encryption protects confidentiality when an adversary gains physical possession of storage, an attack path that bypasses every OS-level access control. Pre-boot authentication (TPM + PIN) defends against cold-boot, DMA and TPM-sniffing attacks that defeat TPM-only configurations. Maps primarily to SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest). Assess key escrow and recovery procedures as well, because an unrecoverable key is an availability risk.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1005 Data from Local System; T1200 Hardware Additions; T1552 Unsecured Credentials

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001199**: Protects the confidentiality and/or integrity of organization-defined information at rest.  
  Rev 5: SC-28 · Rev 4: SC-28 · Rev 3: SC-28
- **CCI-002475**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized modification of organization-defined information at rest on organization-defined system components.  
  Rev 5: SC-28 (1) · Rev 4: SC-28 (1) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002476**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure of organization-defined information at rest on organization-defined system components.  
  Rev 5: SC-28 (1) · Rev 4: SC-28 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-238337 · UBTU-20-010416 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must generate error messages that provide information necessary for corrective actions without revealing information that could be exploited by adversaries.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-238337r1134791_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000205-GPOS-00083 |
| Topic | Audit Log & Tool Protection |
| CCI | CCI-001312 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-11 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-11 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SI-11 b |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate error messages that provide information necessary for corrective actions without revealing information that could be exploited by adversaries.

**Why it matters:** The security diary is only useful if nobody can secretly edit or tear pages out of it. This rule locks down who can read or change the logs and the tools that manage them. It's like keeping the security camera footage in a locked room that only a couple of trusted people can enter.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
find /var/log -perm /137 ! -name '*[bw]tmp' ! -name '*lastlog' -type f -exec stat -c "%n %a" {} \;
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, audit logs live under /var/log/audit/ (mode 0600 or 0640, owned by root, group per log_group). Audit tools are /sbin/auditctl, aureport, ausearch, autrace, auditd, rsyslogd and augenrules (mode 0755, owned by root). '-e 2' at the end of the rules makes the configuration immutable until reboot, and '--loginuid-immutable' prevents processes from changing their audit login UID.

**Operational impact:** With '-e 2', any later audit rule change requires a reboot to take effect, so schedule audit rule updates in maintenance windows.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the Ubuntu operating system has all system log files under the "/var/log" directory with a permission set to "640" or less permissive by using the following command:

Note: The btmp, wtmp, and lastlog files are excluded. Refer to the Discussion for details.

$ sudo find /var/log -perm /137 ! -name '*[bw]tmp' ! -name '*lastlog' -type f -exec stat -c "%n %a" {} \;

If the command displays any output, this is a finding.

Note: If output regarding history.log or eipp.log.xz is displayed, this is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the Ubuntu operating system to set permissions of all log files under the "/var/log" directory to "640" or more restricted by using the following command:

Note: The btmp, wtmp, and lastlog files are excluded. Refer to the Discussion for details.

$ sudo find /var/log -perm /137 ! -name '*[bw]tmp' ! -name '*lastlog' -type f -exec chmod 640 '{}' \;
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Any operating system providing too much information in error messages risks compromising the data and security of the structure, and organizations must carefully consider the content and structure of error messages.

The extent to which information systems are able to identify and handle error conditions is guided by organizational policy and operational requirements. Information that could be exploited by adversaries includes, for example, erroneous logon attempts with passwords entered by mistake as the username, mission/business information that can be derived from (if not stated explicitly by) information recorded, and personal information, such as account numbers, Social Security numbers, and credit card numbers.

The /var/log/btmp, /var/log/wtmp, and /var/log/lastlog files have group write and global read permissions to allow for the lastlog function to perform. Limiting the permissions beyond this configuration will result in the failure of functions that rely on the lastlog database.

**Threat & control context:** If a non-privileged user, or an attacker running as one, can read, alter or delete audit data or reconfigure the audit subsystem, the audit trail loses its evidentiary value. AU-9 (protection of audit information) together with AU-9(3) (cryptographic protection) and AU-9(4) (access by subset of privileged users) require restrictive ownership and modes on logs and tools, integrity verification of audit binaries (via AIDE), and immutable audit rules ('-e 2') so the rule set can't be changed without a reboot.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.002 Indicator Removal: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs; T1070.001 Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001312**: Generate error messages that provide information necessary for corrective actions without revealing information that could be exploited.  
  Rev 5: SI-11 a · Rev 4: SI-11 a · Rev 3: SI-11 b

### V-238338 · UBTU-20-010417 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must configure the /var/log directory to be group-owned by syslog.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-238338r958566_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000206-GPOS-00084 |
| Topic | Audit Log & Tool Protection, Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling |
| CCI | CCI-001314 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-11 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-11 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SI-11 c |
| Implemented via | File permission / ownership / label |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must configure the /var/log directory to be group-owned by syslog.

**Why it matters:** The security diary is only useful if nobody can secretly edit or tear pages out of it. This rule locks down who can read or change the logs and the tools that manage them. It's like keeping the security camera footage in a locked room that only a couple of trusted people can enter.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chgrp | syslog /var/log |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
stat -c "%n %G" /var/log
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo stat -c '%a %U %G %n' /var/log
```

Expected: Mode/owner/group must match: chgrp syslog /var/log.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, audit logs live under /var/log/audit/ (mode 0600 or 0640, owned by root, group per log_group). Audit tools are /sbin/auditctl, aureport, ausearch, autrace, auditd, rsyslogd and augenrules (mode 0755, owned by root). '-e 2' at the end of the rules makes the configuration immutable until reboot, and '--loginuid-immutable' prevents processes from changing their audit login UID.

**Also related (Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling):** auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, disk_full_action, action_mail_acct). Off-load with audisp-remote (package audispd-plugins, configured in /etc/audit/audisp-remote.conf or plugins.d/au-remote.conf) or forward with rsyslog. Install auditd with 'apt-get install auditd audispd-plugins'.

**Operational impact:** With '-e 2', any later audit rule change requires a reboot to take effect, so schedule audit rule updates in maintenance windows.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that the Ubuntu operating system configures the "/var/log" directory to be group-owned by syslog with the following command:

$ sudo stat -c "%n %G" /var/log
/var/log syslog

If the "/var/log" directory is not group-owned by syslog, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the Ubuntu operating system to have syslog group-own the "/var/log" directory by running the following command:

$ sudo chgrp syslog /var/log
```

AU-9 (protection of audit information) together with AU-9(3) (cryptographic protection) and AU-9(4) (access by subset of privileged users) require restrictive ownership and modes on logs and tools, integrity verification of audit binaries (via AIDE), and immutable audit rules ('-e 2') so the rule set can't be changed without a reboot.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.002 Indicator Removal: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs; T1070.001 Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking

'-e 2' at the end of the rules makes the configuration immutable until reboot, and '--loginuid-immutable' prevents processes from changing their audit login UID.

**Also related (Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling):** auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, disk_full_action, action_mail_acct). Off-load with audisp-remote (package audispd-plugins, configured in /etc/audit/audisp-remote.conf or plugins.d/au-remote.conf) or forward with rsyslog. Install auditd with 'apt-get install auditd audispd-plugins'.

**Operational impact:** With '-e 2', any later audit rule change requires a reboot to take effect, so schedule audit rule updates in maintenance windows.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that the Ubuntu operating system configures the "/var/log/syslog" file to be owned by syslog with the following command:

$ sudo stat -c "%n %U" /var/log/syslog
/var/log/syslog syslog

If the "/var/log/syslog" file is not owned by syslog, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the Ubuntu operating system to have syslog own the "/var/log/syslog" file by running the following command:

$ sudo chown syslog /var/log/syslog
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Only authorized personnel should be aware of errors and the details of the errors. Error messages are an indicator of an organization's operational state or can identify the operating system or platform. Additionally, Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and operational information must not be revealed through error messages to unauthorized personnel or their designated representatives.

The structure and content of error messages must be carefully considered by the organization and development team. The extent to which the information system is able to identify and handle error conditions is guided by organizational policy and operational requirements.

**Threat & control context:** If a non-privileged user, or an attacker running as one, can read, alter or delete audit data or reconfigure the audit subsystem, the audit trail loses its evidentiary value. AU-9 (protection of audit information) together with AU-9(3) (cryptographic protection) and AU-9(4) (access by subset of privileged users) require restrictive ownership and modes on logs and tools, integrity verification of audit binaries (via AIDE), and immutable audit rules ('-e 2') so the rule set can't be changed without a reboot.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.002 Indicator Removal: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs; T1070.001 Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001314**: Reveal error messages only to organization-defined personnel or roles.  
  Rev 5: SI-11 b · Rev 4: SI-11 b · Rev 3: SI-11 c

### V-238344 · UBTU-20-010423 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must have directories that contain system commands set to a mode of 0755 or less permissive.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-238344r991559_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000258-GPOS-00099 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-001495 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-9 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-9 |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have directories that contain system commands set to a mode of 0755 or less permissive.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
find /bin /sbin /usr/bin /usr/sbin /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin -perm /022 -type d -exec stat -c "%n %a" '{}' \;
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Check mode and ownership with 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' and fix them with 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp'. Find unowned files with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup'. Default permissions for new files come from UMASK in /etc/login.defs. 'dpkg --verify' highlights packaged files that have changed.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the system commands directories have mode 0755 or less permissive:

/bin
/sbin
/usr/bin
/usr/sbin
/usr/local/bin
/usr/local/sbin

Check that the system command directories have mode 0755 or less permissive with the following command:

$ find /bin /sbin /usr/bin /usr/sbin /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin -perm /022 -type d -exec stat -c "%n %a" '{}' \;

If any directories are found to be group-writable or world-writable, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the system commands directories to be protected from unauthorized access. Run the following command:

$ sudo find /bin /sbin /usr/bin /usr/sbin /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin -perm /022 -type d -exec chmod -R 755 '{}' \;
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Protecting audit information also includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manipulate log data. Therefore, protecting audit tools is necessary to prevent unauthorized operation on audit information.

Operating systems providing tools to interface with audit information will leverage user permissions and roles identifying the user accessing the tools and the corresponding rights the user has in order to make access decisions regarding the deletion of audit tools.

Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open source audit tools needed to successfully view and manipulate audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001495**: Protect audit tools from unauthorized deletion.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9

| Field | Value |

| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-5 (6) |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer library files must be owned by root.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
find /lib /lib64 /usr/lib /usr/lib64 -type f -name '*.so*' ! -user root -exec stat -c "%n %U" {} +
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Check mode and ownership with 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' and fix them with 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp'. Find unowned files with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup'. Default permissions for new files come from UMASK in /etc/login.defs. 'dpkg --verify' highlights packaged files that have changed.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the systemwide shared library files contained in the directories "/lib", "/lib64", "/usr/lib", and "/usr/lib64" are owned by root with the following command:

$ sudo find /lib /lib64 /usr/lib /usr/lib64 -type f -name '*.so*' ! -user root -exec stat -c "%n %U" {} +

If any output is returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the systemwide shared library files contained in the directories "/lib", "/lib64", "/usr/lib", and "/usr/lib64" to be owned by root with the following command:

$ sudo find /lib /lib64 /usr/lib /usr/lib64 -type f -name '*.so*' ! -user root -exec chown root {} +
```

### V-238353 · UBTU-20-010432 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must be configured to preserve log records from failure events.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-238353r991562_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000269-GPOS-00103 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling |
| CCI | CCI-001665 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-24 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-24 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-24 |
| Implemented via | Service (systemd), Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to preserve log records from failure events.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | apt | rsyslog | Installed |
| Service | systemd | rsyslog | enable (now) |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
dpkg -l | grep rsyslog
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
systemctl is-enabled rsyslog
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
systemctl is-active rsyslog
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
dpkg -l rsyslog 2>/dev/null | grep '^ii' || echo 'package rsyslog is not installed'
```

Expected: Package must be installed.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
systemctl is-enabled rsyslog; systemctl is-active rsyslog
```

Expected: Expect enabled / active.

**How it works:** auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, disk_full_action, action_mail_acct). Off-load with audisp-remote (package audispd-plugins, configured in /etc/audit/audisp-remote.conf or plugins.d/au-remote.conf) or forward with rsyslog. Install auditd with 'apt-get install auditd audispd-plugins'.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the log service is configured to collect system failure events.

Check that the log service is installed properly with the following command:

$ dpkg -l | grep rsyslog

ii  rsyslog                                    8.32.0-1ubuntu4                                 amd64        reliable system and kernel logging daemon

If the "rsyslog" package is not installed, this is a finding.

Check that the log service is enabled with the following command:

$ systemctl is-enabled rsyslog

enabled

If the command above returns "disabled", this is a finding.

Check that the log service is properly running and active on the system with the following command:

$ systemctl is-active rsyslog

active

If the command above returns "inactive", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the log service to collect failure events.

Install the log service (if the log service is not already installed) with the following command:

$ sudo apt-get install rsyslog

Enable the log service with the following command:

$ sudo systemctl enable --now rsyslog
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Failure to a known state can address safety or security in accordance with the mission/business needs of the organization. Failure to a known secure state helps prevent a loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability in the event of a failure of the information system or a component of the system.

Preserving operating system state information helps to facilitate operating system restart and return to the operational mode of the organization with least disruption to mission/business processes.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001665**: Preserve organization-defined system state information in the event of a system failure.  
  Rev 5: SC-24 · Rev 4: SC-24 · Rev 3: SC-24

### V-238354 · UBTU-20-010433 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must have an application firewall installed in order to control remote access methods.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-238354r958672_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000297-GPOS-00115 |
| Topic | Host Firewall, Remote Desktop & Remote Management |
| CCI | CCI-002314 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-17 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-17 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have an application firewall installed in order to control remote access methods.

**Why it matters:** A firewall is a gatekeeper that decides which network connections are allowed in and out of the computer. This rule makes sure the gatekeeper is switched on and turns away anything that isn't on the approved list, like a security guard who only lets in people with an appointment.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Firewall*: A filter that decides which network connections are allowed in or out.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | apt | ufw | Installed |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
dpkg -l | grep ufw
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
dpkg -l ufw 2>/dev/null | grep '^ii' || echo 'package ufw is not installed'
```

Expected: Package must be installed.

**How it works:** Ubuntu uses UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) as the front end to nftables or iptables. Install and enable it with 'apt-get install ufw' and 'ufw enable', set default-deny with 'ufw default deny incoming', and allow only the required services ('ufw allow <port>/<proto>', or 'ufw limit ssh' for rate limiting). Review with 'ufw status verbose'.

**Also related (Remote Desktop & Remote Management):** On Ubuntu, X11 forwarding ('X11Forwarding no' in sshd), VNC servers and cockpit are the main remote-access paths to restrict.

**Operational impact:** An over-restrictive default can cut off management or application traffic. Make changes from the console, or stage them with a timed rollback ('firewall-cmd --timeout').

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that the Uncomplicated Firewall is installed with the following command:

$ dpkg -l | grep ufw

ii  ufw         0.36-6

If the "ufw" package is not installed, ask the System Administrator if another application firewall is installed.

If no application firewall is installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install the Uncomplicated Firewall by using the following command:

$ sudo apt-get install ufw
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Remote access services, such as those providing remote access to network devices and information systems, which lack automated control capabilities, increase risk and make remote user access management difficult at best.

Remote access is access to DoD nonpublic information systems by an authorized user (or an information system) communicating through an external, non-organization-controlled network. Remote access methods include, for example, dial-up, broadband, and wireless.

Ubuntu operating system functionality (e.g., RDP) must be capable of taking enforcement action if the audit reveals unauthorized activity. Automated control of remote access sessions allows organizations to ensure ongoing compliance with remote access policies by enforcing connection rules of remote access applications on a variety of information system components (e.g., servers, workstations, notebook computers, smartphones, and tablets).

**Threat & control context:** A host firewall enforces deny-by-default, allow-by-exception at the endpoint (SC-7(5)) and contains lateral movement even when the perimeter is breached or the host sits on a flat network. Exposed ports must match the system's PPSM registration (CM-7(1)). Remote-management exceptions should be scoped to authorized management hosts rather than 'any'. Check that the firewall service can't be stopped by non-administrators and that rule changes are audited.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.004 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall; T1021 Remote Services; T1046 Network Service Discovery; T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol; T1021.006 Remote Services: Windows Remote Management; T1563 Remote Service Session Hijacking; T1040 Network Sniffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002314**: Employ automated mechanisms to control remote access methods.  
  Rev 5: AC-17 (1) · Rev 4: AC-17 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-17 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Service (systemd) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enable and run the uncomplicated firewall(ufw).

**Why it matters:** A firewall is a gatekeeper that decides which network connections are allowed in and out of the computer. This rule makes sure the gatekeeper is switched on and turns away anything that isn't on the approved list, like a security guard who only lets in people with an appointment.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Firewall*: A filter that decides which network connections are allowed in or out.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Service | systemd | ufw.service | enable (now) |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
systemctl is-enabled ufw
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
systemctl is-active ufw
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
systemctl is-enabled ufw.service; systemctl is-active ufw.service
```

Expected: Expect enabled / active.

**How it works:** Ubuntu uses UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) as the front end to nftables or iptables. Install and enable it with 'apt-get install ufw' and 'ufw enable', set default-deny with 'ufw default deny incoming', and allow only the required services ('ufw allow <port>/<proto>', or 'ufw limit ssh' for rate limiting). Review with 'ufw status verbose'.

**Operational impact:** An over-restrictive default can cut off management or application traffic. Make changes from the console, or stage them with a timed rollback ('firewall-cmd --timeout').

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the Uncomplicated Firewall is enabled on the system by running the following command:

$ systemctl is-enabled ufw

If the above command returns the status as "disabled", this is a finding.

Verify the Uncomplicated Firewall is active on the system by running the following command:

$ systemctl is-active ufw

If the above command returns "inactive" or any kind of error, this is a finding.

If the Uncomplicated Firewall is not installed, ask the System Administrator if another application firewall is installed.

If no application firewall is installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Enable the Uncomplicated Firewall by using the following command:

$ sudo systemctl enable --now ufw.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Remote access services, such as those providing remote access to network devices and information systems, which lack automated control capabilities, increase risk and make remote user access management difficult at best.

Remote access is access to DoD nonpublic information systems by an authorized user (or an information system) communicating through an external, non-organization-controlled network. Remote access methods include, for example, dial-up, broadband, and wireless.

Ubuntu operating system functionality (e.g., RDP) must be capable of taking enforcement action if the audit reveals unauthorized activity. Automated control of remote access sessions allows organizations to ensure ongoing compliance with remote access policies by enforcing connection rules of remote access applications on a variety of information system components (e.g., servers, workstations, notebook computers, smartphones, and tablets).

**Threat & control context:** A host firewall enforces deny-by-default, allow-by-exception at the endpoint (SC-7(5)) and contains lateral movement even when the perimeter is breached or the host sits on a flat network. Exposed ports must match the system's PPSM registration (CM-7(1)). Remote-management exceptions should be scoped to authorized management hosts rather than 'any'. Check that the firewall service can't be stopped by non-administrators and that rule changes are audited.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.004 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall; T1021 Remote Services; T1046 Network Service Discovery

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002314**: Employ automated mechanisms to control remote access methods.  
  Rev 5: AC-17 (1) · Rev 4: AC-17 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-238356 · UBTU-20-010435 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must, for networked systems, compare internal information system clocks at least every 24 hours with a server which is synchronized to one of the redundant United States Naval Observatory (USNO) time servers, or a time server designated for the appropriate DoD network (NIPRNet/SIPRNet), and/or the Global Positioning System (GPS).

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-238356r1038944_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000355-GPOS-00143 |
| Topic | Time Synchronization, Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features |
| CCI | CCI-001891, CCI-004923 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-45 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-8 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must, for networked systems, compare internal information system clocks at least every 24 hours with a server which is synchronized to one of the redundant United States Naval Observatory (USNO) time servers, or a time server designated for the appropriate DoD network (NIPRNet/SIPRNet), and/or the Global Positioning System (GPS).

**Why it matters:** This keeps the computer's clock exactly in step with an official time source. That might sound minor, but security logs from different computers can only be pieced together if every clock agrees, and some sign-in systems refuse to work when clocks drift. It's like making sure all the witnesses' watches show the same time.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).
- *NTP / chrony*: Network Time Protocol: how computers keep their clocks accurate over the network.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/chrony/chrony.conf | server | [source] iburst maxpoll = 16 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep  maxpoll /etc/chrony/chrony.conf
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i server /etc/chrony/chrony.conf
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*server\b' /etc/chrony/chrony.conf
```

Expected: server [source] iburst maxpoll = 16

**How it works:** Ubuntu uses chrony (or systemd-timesyncd by default on some releases). For chrony, configure /etc/chrony/chrony.conf with 'server <DoD-time-source> iburst maxpoll 16' and 'makestep 1 -1', and disable systemd-timesyncd so the two don't conflict. Verify with 'chronyc sources -v' and 'timedatectl'.

**Also related (Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features):** On Ubuntu, the equivalents are disabling Apport crash reporting ('systemctl disable --now apport'), the 'ubuntu-report' and popularity-contest data collection, MOTD news ('ENABLED=0' in /etc/default/motd-news), and GNOME online accounts if they're not approved.

**Operational impact:** Large clock corrections can confuse running applications. chrony slews gradually by default. Make sure the time servers are reachable through the firewall (UDP 123).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the system is not networked, this requirement is Not Applicable.

The system clock must be configured to compare the system clock at least every 24 hours to the authoritative time source.

Check the value of "maxpoll" in the "/etc/chrony/chrony.conf" file with the following command:

$ sudo  grep  maxpoll /etc/chrony/chrony.conf
server tick.usno.navy.mil iburst maxpoll 16

If the "maxpoll" option is set to a number greater than 16 or the line is commented out, this is a finding.

Verify that the "chrony.conf" file is configured to an authoritative DoD time source by running the following command:

$ grep -i server /etc/chrony/chrony.conf
server tick.usno.navy.mil iburst maxpoll 16
server tock.usno.navy.mil iburst maxpoll 16
server ntp2.usno.navy.mil iburst maxpoll 16

If the parameter "server" is not set, is not set to an authoritative DoD time source, or is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the system is not networked, this requirement is Not Applicable.

To configure the system clock to compare the system clock at least every 24 hours to the authoritative time source, edit the "/etc/chrony/chrony.conf" file. Add or correct the following lines, by replacing "[source]" in the following line with an authoritative DoD time source:

server [source] iburst maxpoll = 16

If the "chrony" service was running and the value of "maxpoll" or "server" was updated, the service must be restarted using the following command:

$ sudo systemctl restart chrony.service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inaccurate time stamps make it more difficult to correlate events and can lead to an inaccurate analysis. Determining the correct time a particular event occurred on a system is critical when conducting forensic analysis and investigating system events. Sources outside the configured acceptable allowance (drift) may be inaccurate.

Synchronizing internal information system clocks provides uniformity of time stamps for information systems with multiple system clocks and systems connected over a network.

Organizations should consider endpoints that may not have regular access to the authoritative time server (e.g., mobile, teleworking, and tactical endpoints).

**Threat & control context:** Accurate, synchronized time underpins log correlation across systems, Kerberos authentication (5-minute skew tolerance), certificate validity checks and forensic timelines (AU-8, AU-8(1) synchronization with an authoritative source, AU-8(2) secondary source). Time sources should be authenticated where possible and restricted to client mode, so the host can't be abused as an NTP amplifier.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.006 Indicator Removal: Timestomp; T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001891**: The information system compares internal information system clocks on an organization-defined frequency with an organization-defined authoritative time source.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: AU-8 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-004923**: Compare the internal system clocks on an organization-defined frequency with organization-defined authoritative time source.  
  Rev 5: SC-45 (1) (a) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-238359 · UBTU-20-010438 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system's Advance Package Tool (APT) must be configured to prevent the installation of patches, service packs, device drivers, or Ubuntu operating system components without verification they have been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-238359r1015157_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000366-GPOS-00153 |
| Topic | Software & File Integrity Verification, Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication |
| CCI | CCI-001749, CCI-003992 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-14 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-5 (3) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer 's Advance Package Tool (APT) must be configured to prevent the installation of patches, service packs, device drivers, or this computer components without verification they have been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.

**Why it matters:** This makes the computer check a digital "seal" on software before installing it, and keep a fingerprint of important files so it can notice if anyone changes them. It's like checking that a medicine bottle's safety seal is intact, and noticing straight away if someone has tampered with it.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PKI / certificates*: Public Key Infrastructure: the system of digital ID certificates and trusted issuers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep AllowUnauthenticated /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/*
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** APT verifies repository signatures with the keys in /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/ and per-source 'signed-by' keyrings, so never add '[trusted=yes]' or '--allow-unauthenticated'. Install AIDE with 'apt-get install aide aide-common', initialize with 'aideinit', and configure rules in /etc/aide/aide.conf. A daily check runs from /etc/cron.daily/dailyaidecheck. 'dpkg --verify' checks installed files against package checksums.

**Also related (Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication):** Ubuntu uses libpam-pkcs11 and opensc-pkcs11 for CAC/PIV login: a pam_pkcs11.so line in /etc/pam.d/common-auth, certificate mapping and OCSP/CRL policy in /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf, and DoD CA certificates installed under /etc/ssl/certs (or /usr/local/share/ca-certificates followed by 'update-ca-certificates').

**Operational impact:** AIDE reports every legitimate change too, so re-baseline after approved patching and keep the database read-only or off-host. Internal repositories must sign their packages, or clients will refuse them.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that APT is configured to prevent the installation of patches, service packs, device drivers, or Ubuntu operating system components without verification they have been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.

Check that the "AllowUnauthenticated" variable is not set at all or is set to "false" with the following command:

$ grep AllowUnauthenticated /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/*
/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/01-vendor-Ubuntu:APT::Get::AllowUnauthenticated "false";

If any of the files returned from the command with "AllowUnauthenticated" are set to "true", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure APT to prevent the installation of patches, service packs, device drivers, or Ubuntu operating system components without verification they have been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.

Remove/update any APT configuration files that contain the variable "AllowUnauthenticated" to "false", or remove "AllowUnauthenticated" entirely from each file. Below is an example of setting the "AllowUnauthenticated" variable to "false":

APT::Get::AllowUnauthenticated "false";
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Changes to any software components can have significant effects on the overall security of the operating system. This requirement ensures the software has not been tampered with and that it has been provided by a trusted vendor.

Accordingly, patches, service packs, device drivers, or operating system components must be signed with a certificate recognized and approved by the organization.

Verifying the authenticity of the software prior to installation validates the integrity of the patch or upgrade received from a vendor. This ensures the software has not been tampered with and that it has been provided by a trusted vendor. Self-signed certificates are disallowed by this requirement. The operating system should not have to verify the software again. This requirement does not mandate DoD certificates for this purpose; however, the certificate used to verify the software must be from an approved CA.

**Threat & control context:** Signature verification ensures only vendor-authentic software is installed (CM-14 signed components, SI-7 software and information integrity). File-integrity monitoring such as AIDE detects unauthorized modification of binaries and configuration after the fact (SI-7(1), CM-3(5)), catching rootkits, backdoored binaries and configuration drift. The value of FIM depends on protecting the baseline database off-host and acting on alerts.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1195 Supply Chain Compromise; T1554 Compromise Host Software Binary; T1014 Rootkit; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001749**: The information system prevents the installation of organization-defined software components without verification the software component has been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: CM-5 (3) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-003992**: Prevent the installation of organization-defined software and firmware components without verification that the component has been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.  
  Rev 5: CM-14 · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-238360 · UBTU-20-010439 · CAT II: The Ubuntu operating system must be configured to use AppArmor.

| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 (2), CM-7 (5) (b), AC-3 (4), AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 (2), CM-7 (5) (b), AC-3 (4), AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Service (systemd), Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to use AppArmor.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | apt | apparmor | Installed |
| Service | systemd | apparmor.service | enable |
| Service | systemd | apparmor.service | start |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
dpkg -l | grep apparmor
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
systemctl is-active apparmor.service
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
systemctl is-enabled apparmor.service
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
dpkg -l apparmor 2>/dev/null | grep '^ii' || echo 'package apparmor is not installed'
```

Expected: Package must be installed.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
systemctl is-enabled apparmor.service; systemctl is-active apparmor.service
```

Expected: Expect enabled / active.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the operating system prevents program execution in accordance with local policies.

Check that AppArmor is installed and active by running the following command,

$ dpkg -l | grep apparmor

If the "apparmor" package is not installed, this is a finding.

$ systemctl is-active apparmor.service

active

If "active" is not returned, this is a finding.

$ systemctl is-enabled apparmor.service

enabled

If "enabled" is not returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install "AppArmor" (if it is not installed) with the following command:

$ sudo apt-get install apparmor

$ sudo systemctl enable apparmor.service

Start "apparmor" with the following command:

$ sudo systemctl start apparmor.service

Note: AppArmor must have properly configured profiles for applications and home directories. All configurations will be based on the actual system setup and organization and normally are on a per role basis. See the AppArmor documentation for more information on configuring profiles.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Control of program execution is a mechanism used to prevent execution of unauthorized programs. Some operating systems may provide a capability that runs counter to the mission or provides users with functionality that exceeds mission requirements. This includes functions and services installed at the operating system-level.

Some of the programs, installed by default, may be harmful or may not be necessary to support essential organizational operations (e.g., key missions, functions). Removal of executable programs is not always possible; therefore, establishing a method of preventing program execution is critical to maintaining a secure system baseline.

Methods for complying with this requirement include restricting execution of programs in certain environments, while preventing execution in other environments; or limiting execution of certain program functionality based on organization-defined criteria (e.g., privileges, subnets, sandboxed environments, or roles).

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000368-GPOS-00154, SRG-OS-000312-GPOS-00122, SRG-OS-000312-GPOS-00123, SRG-OS-000312-GPOS-00124, SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125, SRG-OS-000370-GPOS-00155

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001764**: Prevent program execution in accordance with organization-defined policies, rules of behavior, and/or access agreements regarding software program usage and restrictions; rules authorizing the terms and conditions of software program usage.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (2) · Rev 4: CM-7 (2) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001774**: Employ a deny-all, permit-by-exception policy to allow the execution of authorized software programs on the system.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (5) (b) · Rev 4: CM-7 (5) (b) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002165**: Enforce organization-defined discretionary access control policies over defined subjects and objects.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 (4) · Rev 4: AC-3 (4) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.

### V-238362 · UBTU-20-010441 · CAT III: The Ubuntu operating system must be configured such that Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) prohibits the use of cached authentications after one day.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-238362r958828_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000383-GPOS-00166 |
| Topic | Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-002007 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (13) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (13) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured such that Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) prohibits the use of cached authentications after one day.

**Why it matters:** Behind the sign-in screen is a chain of checks: the password is right, the account isn't locked, the password isn't expired, and so on. This rule makes sure every check in that chain is present and in the correct order, like making sure every guard at a multi-checkpoint entrance is at their post.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.
- *SSSD*: A Linux service that connects the computer to a central user directory and handles sign-ins.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/sssd/sssd.conf | offline_credentials_expiration | 1 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep offline_credentials_expiration /etc/sssd/sssd.conf /etc/sssd/conf.d/*.conf
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*offline_credentials_expiration\b' /etc/sssd/sssd.conf
```

Expected: offline_credentials_expiration = 1

**How it works:** Ubuntu's PAM stacks are /etc/pam.d/common-auth, common-account, common-password and common-session. They are regenerated by 'pam-auth-update' from profiles in /usr/share/pam-configs/, so persistent changes belong in a custom profile there or must be re-checked after package updates. SSSD (if used) is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf (mode 0600, owned by root).

**Operational impact:** PAM mistakes can lock everyone out, including root. Test changes from a second, still-open root session, and keep console access available.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If smart card authentication is not being used on the system, this s Not Applicable.

Verify that PAM prohibits the use of cached authentications after one day with the following command:

$ sudo grep offline_credentials_expiration /etc/sssd/sssd.conf /etc/sssd/conf.d/*.conf

offline_credentials_expiration = 1

If "offline_credentials_expiration" is not set to a value of "1" in "/etc/sssd/sssd.conf" or in a file with a name ending in .conf in the "/etc/sssd/conf.d/" directory, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure PAM to prohibit the use of cached authentications after one day. Add or change the following line in "/etc/sssd/sssd.conf" just below the line "[pam]":

offline_credentials_expiration = 1

Note: It is valid for this configuration to be in a file with a name that ends with ".conf" and does not begin with a "." in the "/etc/sssd/conf.d/" directory instead of the "/etc/sssd/sssd.conf" file.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If cached authentication information is out-of-date, the validity of the authentication information may be questionable.

**Threat & control context:** PAM and SSSD define how every Linux authentication decision is made. Misordered or optional modules silently bypass controls such as faillock, pwquality and pwhistory. Credential caching lifetimes trade availability against revocation latency, so a revoked account keeps working offline until its cache expires. These settings support IA-2, IA-5(13) (expiration of cached authenticators), AC-7, AC-9 (previous logon notification) and AC-10 (concurrent session control).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1556.003 Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002007**: Prohibit the use of cached authenticators after an organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (13) · Rev 4: IA-5 (13) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-238363 · UBTU-20-010442 · CAT I: The Ubuntu operating system must implement NIST FIPS-validated cryptography to protect classified information and for the following: To provision digital signatures, to generate cryptographic hashes, and to protect unclassified information requiring confidentiality and cryptographic protection in accordance with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, and standards.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-238363r1014774_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000396-GPOS-00176 |
| Topic | Software & File Integrity Verification, Approved Cryptography (FIPS 140) |
| CCI | CCI-002450 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-13 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-13 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must implement NIST FIPS-validated cryptography to protect classified information and for the following: To provision digital signatures, to generate cryptographic hashes, and to protect unclassified information requiring confidentiality and cryptographic protection in accordance with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, and standards.

**Why it matters:** This makes the computer check a digital "seal" on software before installing it, and keep a fingerprint of important files so it can notice if anyone changes them. It's like checking that a medicine bottle's safety seal is intact, and noticing straight away if someone has tampered with it.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *FIPS 140*: A U.S. government standard for testing and approving encryption software.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i 1 /proc/sys/crypto/fips_enabled
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** APT verifies repository signatures with the keys in /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/ and per-source 'signed-by' keyrings, so never add '[trusted=yes]' or '--allow-unauthenticated'. Install AIDE with 'apt-get install aide aide-common', initialize with 'aideinit', and configure rules in /etc/aide/aide.conf. A daily check runs from /etc/cron.daily/dailyaidecheck. 'dpkg --verify' checks installed files against package checksums.

**Also related (Approved Cryptography (FIPS 140)):** Ubuntu provides FIPS 140-validated modules through Ubuntu Pro: 'pro enable fips-updates' (or 'fips'), then reboot into the FIPS kernel. Verify with 'cat /proc/sys/crypto/fips_enabled' (expect 1). sshd ciphers, MACs and key exchange algorithms are set explicitly in /etc/ssh/sshd_config, because Ubuntu has no RHEL-style system-wide crypto-policies.

**Operational impact:** AIDE reports every legitimate change too, so re-baseline after approved patching and keep the database read-only or off-host. Internal repositories must sign their packages, or clients will refuse them.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the system is configured to run in FIPS mode with the following command:

$ grep -i 1 /proc/sys/crypto/fips_enabled
1

If a value of "1" is not returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the system to run in FIPS mode. Add "fips=1" to the kernel parameter during the Ubuntu operating systems install.

Enabling a FIPS mode on a pre-existing system involves a number of modifications to the Ubuntu operating system. Refer to the Ubuntu Server 20.04 FIPS 140-2 security policy document for instructions.

A subscription to the "Ubuntu Pro" plan is required to obtain the FIPS Kernel cryptographic modules and enable FIPS.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Use of weak or untested encryption algorithms undermines the purposes of utilizing encryption to protect data. The operating system must implement cryptographic modules adhering to the higher standards approved by the federal government since this provides assurance they have been tested and validated.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000396-GPOS-00176, SRG-OS-000478-GPOS-00223

**Threat & control context:** Signature verification ensures only vendor-authentic software is installed (CM-14 signed components, SI-7 software and information integrity). File-integrity monitoring such as AIDE detects unauthorized modification of binaries and configuration after the fact (SI-7(1), CM-3(5)), catching rootkits, backdoored binaries and configuration drift. The value of FIM depends on protecting the baseline database off-host and acting on alerts.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1195 Supply Chain Compromise; T1554 Compromise Host Software Binary; T1014 Rootkit; T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002450**: Implement organization-defined types of cryptography for each specified cryptography use.  
  Rev 5: SC-13 b · Rev 4: SC-13 · Rev 3: n/a
